needs_owner.model_text: By default, PostgreSQL will NOT give up on its own after a fixed period. The lock_timeout setting controls how long a statement waits to acquire a lock before erroring out, but its default value is 0, and 0 means the timeout is disabled — there is no limit, so the statement waits indefinitely for the lock. The only mechanisms that could still cause the wait to end are: deadlock_timeout (default 1s), which triggers deadlock detection (not a general timeout, only cancels if an actual deadlock cycle is found), or statement_timeout (also default 0/disabled) if separately configured. So a migration statement blocked behind a long-running query's lock will simply hang until the lock is released, the client disconnects, or an admin intervenes — unless lock_timeout or statement_timeout is explicitly set to a nonzero value.

needs_owner.primary_source_fact: lock_timeout -- "Abort any statement that waits longer than the specified amount of time while attempting to acquire a lock on a table, index, row, or other database object. The time limit applies separately to each lock acquisition attempt. ... If this value is specified without units, it is taken as milliseconds. A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout."

needs_owner.model_text: By default, PostgreSQL does not automatically give up waiting for a lock. A migration statement (e.g., ALTER TABLE) that needs a lock held by a long-running query will simply block and wait until the lock is released, potentially indefinitely, unless something external intervenes. This behavior is controlled by the lock_timeout setting, whose default value is 0. A value of 0 means the timeout is disabled — there is no maximum time a statement will wait to acquire a lock before erroring out. This differs from statement_timeout, which limits total statement execution time regardless of locks. To make migrations fail fast instead of hanging or blocking other queries, administrators often explicitly set lock_timeout (e.g., SET lock_timeout = '5s';) for the migration session.

Isolation level is ISOLATION_DEFAULT — the default isolation level of the underlying datastore is used, rather than Spring imposing a specific level. Read-write mode: the transaction is read-write (readOnly defaults to false). Timeout: no timeout is applied by Spring itself; the default timeout of the underlying transaction system is used (i.e., effectively none set by the annotation). These are the defaults defined on the @Transactional annotation attributes (propagation, isolation, readOnly, timeout) when none are explicitly specified.

needs_owner.model_text: RFC 9700 mandates PKCE (RFC 7636) for all clients using the authorization code grant, including public clients like your mobile app, to protect against authorization code injection/interception. This isn't optional for public clients — it's a baseline requirement regardless of client type. Separately, RFC 9700 explicitly says the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant must not be used. It exposes the user's credentials directly to your app, offers no phishing resistance, is incompatible with MFA and other modern auth methods, and the OAuth 2.0 framework itself deprecates it. For your mobile app, use the authorization code grant with PKCE and a system browser or secure web view (per RFC 8252 for native apps), not ROPC.

needs_owner.model_text:
RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice) mandates that all OAuth clients using the authorization code grant—public and confidential alike—use PKCE, to prevent authorization code injection/interception attacks. For a public mobile client with no client secret, PKCE (with S256 code_challenge_method) is required, and it should also use the system browser (not an embedded webview) per related BCPs. Regarding the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant: RFC 9700 explicitly states that ROPC 'MUST NOT be used' — it's deprecated. Reasons include: it exposes raw user credentials to the client app, offers no support for MFA/federated/social login, trains users to enter passwords into third-party apps (phishing risk), and provides no mechanism for consent or token scoping comparable to redirect-based flows. Instead, use the Authorization Code grant with PKCE via the system browser or an in-app browser tab (e.g., AppAuth pattern), which keeps credential entry on the identity provider's own trusted surface.

needs_owner.model_text: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW without CONCURRENTLY acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the materialized view. This is the strictest lock mode in PostgreSQL and conflicts with every other lock mode, including ACCESS SHARE, which is what a plain SELECT takes. As a result, a SELECT issued against the materialized view while the refresh is running will block and wait until the refresh transaction commits (or rolls back). The dashboard will stall for the duration of the refresh. If concurrent read access during refresh is required, the operator should use REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY instead, which takes a less restrictive lock (roughly EXCLUSIVE, not ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) and allows concurrent SELECTs to proceed, though it requires a unique index on the materialized view and is typically slower because it computes a diff.

needs_owner.model_text:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the table. This mode doesn't conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE (the lock INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE take), so concurrent DML proceeds normally - only conflicts with other DDL-ish operations (another CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM FULL, ALTER TABLE, etc.). 'Non-blocking' is accurate here.

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY takes an EXCLUSIVE lock on the materialized view. EXCLUSIVE conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE, so if DML were attempted it would block. But materialized views aren't directly writable via INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE regardless of locking - they're read-only except through REFRESH. So the real effect of CONCURRENTLY here is allowing concurrent SELECT (ACCESS SHARE) reads, which a plain REFRESH (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) would block. Calling it 'non-blocking' for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE is misleading/inapplicable; it should be described as 'allows concurrent reads' instead.

needs_owner.primary_source_fact: SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE: "Acquired by VACUUM (without FULL), ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, CREATE STATISTICS, COMMENT ON, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, and certain ALTER INDEX and ALTER TABLE variants". EXCLUSIVE: "This mode allows only concurrent ACCESS SHARE locks, i.e., only reads from the table can proceed in parallel with a transaction holding this lock mode." / "Acquired by REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY."

needs_owner.model_text:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY acquires a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the target table. This mode conflicts with itself and with other DDL-ish locks (VACUUM FULL, ALTER TABLE, another CONCURRENTLY build) but does not conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE, so concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (and SELECT) proceed normally — 'non-blocking' is an accurate description for DML here.

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY acquires an ExclusiveLock on the materialized view (versus AccessExclusiveLock for a plain REFRESH). However, materialized views are not directly writable — you cannot INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into one — so the 'concurrent DML' question doesn't apply. What CONCURRENTLY actually buys you is that SELECT (AccessShareLock) can still run against the matview while the refresh proceeds, since plain REFRESH's AccessExclusiveLock would block even reads. So the ticket's 'non-blocking' claim is valid for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY w.r.t. writes, but for the REFRESH statement it should instead be framed as 'non-blocking for reads' — there's no DML to block in the first place.

needs_owner.expected_proposition: An updating command under READ COMMITTED can observe an inconsistent snapshot: the effects of concurrent updates on the rows it is updating, but not their effects on other rows -- so a multi-row conditional update is not made safe by the re-evaluation.
needs_owner.model_text: No, T1 does not apply its update to that row. In READ COMMITTED, when an UPDATE blocks on a row locked by a concurrent transaction, it waits for that transaction to finish. If the blocking transaction commits, PostgreSQL does not simply proceed with the original snapshot's row version — it performs an EvalPlanQual (EPQ) check: it fetches the newest committed version of the row and re-evaluates the UPDATE's WHERE clause against that new version. Here, T2 changed status to 'closed', so the predicate status = 'open' no longer holds, and PostgreSQL silently skips updating that row (it is excluded from the result set, not an error). This means simple conditional counter updates are already safe from applying stale-predicate writes under READ COMMITTED; FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE would mainly matter for cross-row invariants or avoiding the wait/retry pattern itself, not this single-row predicate race.
needs_owner.source_locator: PostgreSQL 18 documentation, section 13.2.1 Read Committed Isolation Level
needs_owner.primary_source_fact: "If the first updater commits, the second updater will ignore the row if the first updater deleted it, otherwise it will attempt to apply its operation to the updated version of the row. The search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches the search condition. If so, the second updater proceeds with its operation using the updated version of the row." and "it is possible for an updating command to see an inconsistent snapshot: it can see the effects of concurrent updating commands on the same rows it is trying to update, but it does not see effects of those commands on other rows in the database."
needs_owner.reason_adjudication_required: The claim is an explanation of a consequence, not a value. There is no boolean or enum whose equality decides whether a given wording conveys it, and scoring it lexically is exactly the substring matching that produced a false headline in Sprint 5 (SPRINT5_RESULTS.md §6).

needs_owner.expected_proposition: An updating command under READ COMMITTED can observe an inconsistent snapshot: the effects of concurrent updates on the rows it is updating, but not their effects on other rows -- so a multi-row conditional update is not made safe by the re-evaluation.
needs_owner.model_text:
No. In READ COMMITTED, when T1's UPDATE finds the target row locked by T2, it blocks on that row's lock. Once T2 commits, T1 doesn't blindly proceed with its original snapshot of the row — PostgreSQL re-fetches the latest committed version of that row and re-evaluates the UPDATE's WHERE clause against it (the EvalPlanQual mechanism). Since T2 set status='closed', the predicate status='open' now fails for that row, so T1 silently skips it — no increment is applied, no error is raised. (If T2 had instead rolled back, T1 would re-check against the original 'open' row and proceed to update it.) needs_owner.model_text: Because both methods use REQUIRED and the inner bean call goes through its own transactional proxy, the inner transaction joins the single existing physical transaction (1 physical transaction total). When the inner method throws a RuntimeException, Spring's transaction interceptor marks the transaction rollback-only via setRollbackOnly() before the exception propagates to the outer method. The outer method's catch block swallows the exception and returns normally, so no exception leaves the outer method body — but at commit time the outer transactional proxy sees the rollback-only flag and refuses to commit. Instead of committing, it rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException to the outer method's caller. Net effect: no data is committed, and the caller receives an exception they never expected given the try/catch appeared to handle the failure.

This is expected behavior so that the caller of a transaction can never be misled to assume that a commit was performed when it really was not."

needs_owner.model_text: Starting with JDK 18, JEP 400 ('UTF-8 by Default') made UTF-8 the default charset across all platforms, including Windows. So Charset.defaultCharset() returns UTF-8 even though the system codepage is windows-1252 (Cp1252); the OS codepage is no longer consulted for this. JEP 400 is the specification change, delivered in JDK 18. Passing -Dfile.encoding=<value> on the java command line is an officially supported way to configure file.encoding (and thus influence default-charset-derived behavior), though Charset.defaultCharset() itself is specified to be UTF-8 unless overridden via the special COMPAT token. To restore the previous locale/codepage-dependent behavior (native encoding, e.g. windows-1252 on this system), set -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT. For the FileWriter scenario, best practice is still to avoid relying on default charset and instead use explicit-charset constructors (e.g., new OutputStreamWriter(..., StandardCharsets.UTF_8) or the JDK 11+ FileWriter(file, Charset) overload) so behavior is deterministic across JDK versions and platforms.

needs_owner.model_text: ConcurrentHashMap provides weakly consistent iterators: concurrent puts/removes during iteration never throw ConcurrentModificationException (unlike HashMap). However, an Iterator instance itself is not thread-safe to share across threads—each Iterator has internal mutable state (next node, current bucket, etc.) with no synchronization, so concurrent calls to next()/remove() on the same iterator from multiple threads can corrupt that state or throw spurious exceptions (e.g., NoSuchElementException). Each thread should obtain its own iterator via map.entrySet().iterator(). Regarding size(): it returns an approximation—CHM computes it from per-segment/counter cells that are updated without full locking, so under concurrent modification size() can be stale or inconsistent with the actual entry count at any instant. It's fine for monitoring/heuristics but should not be relied on for exact program control like triggering an exact-batch-size action; use an explicit counter (e.g., AtomicInteger/LongAdder) or a blocking/bounded structure (e.g., process-and-drain pattern) if precise batch semantics are required.

needs_owner.model_text: Per RFC 9111, Cache-Control: no-cache on a response does NOT forbid a cache from storing it. A cache may store a response marked no-cache; what no-cache forbids is reusing that stored response to satisfy a later request without first successfully revalidating it with the origin server (e.g., via a conditional request). So the answer to the third question is no: a cache may not reuse a no-cache response to satisfy a later request without contacting (revalidating with) the origin server. The directive that actually forbids storage is no-store — a cache must not store any part of either the request or the response. For an authenticated page with personal data that must not be retained by caches at all, the reviewer should use Cache-Control: no-store (often combined with private), not no-cache, since no-cache still permits the response to sit in a cache's storage indefinitely, just not be served without revalidation.

needs_owner.model_text: RFC 9700 (BCP 240) treats the two grants differently. For the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant, the RFC uses the strongest prohibition keyword: clients 'MUST NOT' use it, reflecting that it is considered obsolete and insecure (it exposes the end-user credentials directly to the client, defeats the purpose of delegated authorization, and is incompatible with multi-factor/external authentication). For the implicit grant (response_type=token and other response types that return access tokens directly from the authorization endpoint), the RFC uses a weaker, non-absolute keyword: clients 'SHOULD NOT' use it, because of token leakage/replay risks via the URI fragment and lack of client authentication. Per RFC 2119 semantics, SHOULD NOT permits deviation if the implications are understood and justified by specific circumstances, whereas MUST NOT is an absolute prohibition. So no, the levels are not the same. Practical implication for your review: the mobile app's use of ROPC is a hard violation of the BCP and should be remediated/removed; the SPA's use of implicit flow is a strong recommendation against, but could potentially be defended on a documented, time-boxed basis with compensating controls (e.g., strict redirect URI validation, short token lifetimes, migration plan to Authorization Code + PKCE) — though RFC 9700's clear guidance is to migrate away from implicit as well, since Authorization Code with PKCE is the recommended replacement for both native/mobile and SPA use cases.

rows.baseline_answer_full: PostgreSQL 11+ added the 'fast default' optimization: ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <constant> NOT NULL only updates the table's metadata (pg_attribute) and does not rewrite the table's 400M existing rows; the default is stored and returned for old rows missing the value. rows.governed_answer_full:
Since PG 11, ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <constant> NOT NULL is metadata-only: no table rewrite, no full-table scan — the default is stored in pg_attribute (attmissingval) and existing rows read it virtually. It still takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table, but only briefly (milliseconds) to update the catalog, so it won't block readers/writers for long (though it will queue behind/block concurrent queries momentarily and must wait for existing transactions to finish). Changing the default to clock_timestamp() changes this entirely: it's a volatile function, so Postgres can't treat it as a single constant — it must rewrite the whole table, computing the value per row, holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the full rewrite duration (potentially very long on 400M rows, blocking all reads/writes).

rows.baseline_answer_full: By default, PostgreSQL will NOT give up on its own after a fixed period. The lock_timeout setting controls how long a statement waits to acquire a lock before erroring out, but its default value is 0, and 0 means the timeout is disabled — there is no limit, so the statement waits indefinitely for the lock. The only mechanisms that could still cause the wait to end are: deadlock_timeout (default 1s), which triggers deadlock detection (not a general timeout, only cancels if an actual deadlock cycle is found), or statement_timeout (also default 0/disabled) if separately configured. So a migration statement blocked behind a long-running query's lock will simply hang until the lock is released, the client disconnects, or an admin intervenes — unless lock_timeout or statement_timeout is explicitly set to a nonzero value.

rows.governed_answer_full: By default, PostgreSQL does not automatically give up waiting for a lock. A migration statement (e.g., ALTER TABLE) that needs a lock held by a long-running query will simply block and wait until the lock is released, potentially indefinitely, unless something external intervenes. This behavior is controlled by the lock_timeout setting, whose default value is 0. A value of 0 means the timeout is disabled — there is no maximum time a statement will wait to acquire a lock before erroring out. This differs from statement_timeout, which limits total statement execution time regardless of locks. To make migrations fail fast instead of hanging or blocking other queries, administrators often explicitly set lock_timeout (e.g., SET lock_timeout = '5s';) for the migration session.

When a migration statement in PostgreSQL has to wait for a lock held by a long-running query, does the server give up after some default period on its own? What is the default value of lock_timeout, and what does that value mean? Answer in under 150 words.
deep_consensus_result_object.status_explanation: Every material claim is now AGREED, CORRECTED_AND_AGREED or CONFIRMED_ONE_SIDED after one review round, with nothing left uncompared.
deep_consensus_result_object.verdict: No — by default PostgreSQL waits indefinitely for the lock; lock_timeout defaults to 0, meaning no timeout is applied.
deep_consensus_result_object.governed_answer: By default, PostgreSQL does not automatically give up waiting for a lock. A migration statement (e.g., ALTER TABLE) that needs a lock held by a long-running query will simply block and wait until the lock is released, potentially indefinitely, unless something external intervenes. This behavior is controlled by the lock_timeout setting, whose default value is 0. A value of 0 means the timeout is disabled — there is no maximum time a statement will wait to acquire a lock before erroring out. This differs from statement_timeout, which limits total statement execution time regardless of locks. To make migrations fail fast instead of hanging or blocking other queries, administrators often explicitly set lock_timeout (e.g., SET lock_timeout = '5s';) for the migration session.

These are the defaults defined on the @Transactional annotation attributes (propagation, isolation, readOnly, timeout) when none are explicitly specified.

rows.governed_answer_full: Per the Spring Framework reference documentation, a method annotated with a bare @Transactional (no attributes specified) gets: Propagation setting: REQUIRED (PROPAGATION_REQUIRED) — it joins an existing transaction if one exists, or creates a new one if none exists. Isolation level: DEFAULT (ISOLATION_DEFAULT) — this defers to the underlying datastore/JDBC driver's default isolation level rather than Spring imposing its own. Read-write mode: read-write — the transaction is not marked read-only, so both reads and writes are permitted. Timeout: the default timeout of the underlying transaction system, i.e. no timeout is explicitly set by Spring (represented internally as -1, meaning 'use the default timeout of the transaction system', often effectively no timeout).

rows.baseline_answer_full: At REPEATABLE READ (PostgreSQL's snapshot isolation implementation), when transaction A tries to UPDATE a row that was concurrently updated and committed by transaction B after A's snapshot was taken, PostgreSQL detects that A is trying to modify a row version that is no longer current and that was changed by a transaction that committed after A began. PostgreSQL does not silently apply A's update on top of B's change (that would violate snapshot semantics), nor does it block indefinitely — instead it aborts transaction A with a serialization failure error: 'ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update', SQLSTATE 40001. The application must catch this error, roll back transaction A completely (ROLLBACK), and retry the entire transaction from the beginning (re-reading data and reapplying logic), typically with a retry loop and possibly exponential backoff, since simply re-issuing the same UPDATE won't fix the underlying conflict.

For your mobile app, use the authorization code grant with PKCE and a system browser or secure web view (per RFC 8252 for native apps), not ROPC.

rows.governed_answer_full:
RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice) mandates that all OAuth clients using the authorization code grant—public and confidential alike—use PKCE, to prevent authorization code injection/interception attacks. For a public mobile client with no client secret, PKCE (with S256 code_challenge_method) is required, and it should also use the system browser (not an embedded webview) per related BCPs. Regarding the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant: RFC 9700 explicitly states that ROPC 'MUST NOT be used' — it's deprecated. Reasons include: it exposes raw user credentials to the client app, offers no support for MFA/federated/social login, trains users to enter passwords into third-party apps (phishing risk), and provides no mechanism for consent or token scoping comparable to redirect-based flows. Instead, use the Authorization Code grant with PKCE via the system browser or an in-app browser tab (e.g., AppAuth pattern), which keeps credential entry on the identity provider's own trusted surface.

A.verdict: Yes, PKCE is mandatory for public clients' authorization code grant; ROPC must not be used.
A.answer: RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice) mandates that all OAuth clients using the authorization code grant—public and confidential alike—use PKCE, to prevent authorization code injection/interception attacks. For a public mobile client with no client secret, PKCE (with S256 code_challenge_method) is required, and it should also use the system browser (not an embedded webview) per related BCPs. Regarding the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant: RFC 9700 explicitly states that ROPC 'MUST NOT be used' — it's deprecated. Reasons include: it exposes raw user credentials to the client app, offers no support for MFA/federated/social login, trains users to enter passwords into third-party apps (phishing risk), and provides no mechanism for consent or token scoping comparable to redirect-based flows. Instead, use the Authorization Code grant with PKCE via the system browser or an in-app browser tab (e.g., AppAuth pattern), which keeps credential entry on the identity provider's own trusted surface.

rows.baseline_answer_full: JDK 18 (via JEP 400, 'UTF-8 by Default') changed java.nio.charset.Charset.defaultCharset() to UTF-8 on all platforms, overriding the old behavior where the default was derived from the OS/locale (e.g., windows-1252 or a DBCS codepage on non-UTF-8 Windows locales). This affects any JDK from 18 onward, including 21. APIs like `new FileReader(path)`, `new FileWriter(path)`, and `String.getBytes()`/`new String(byte[])` that rely on the platform default charset will silently switch from the old Windows locale encoding to UTF-8 after the JDK17→21 upgrade. This can cause mojibake or data corruption reading/writing files that were encoded in the old default, or mismatches versus data produced by other non-upgraded processes. Mitigations: explicitly pass charsets, or set `-Dfile.encoding=<old-encoding>` / `-Dsun.jnu.encoding` to preserve old behavior if needed.

rows.governed_answer_full:
Yes, this changes. JEP 400 (JDK 18) made UTF-8 the standard default charset for the JVM on all platforms, replacing the old behavior where the default came from the OS/locale (`file.encoding`). On JDK 17 and earlier, on a Windows host with a non-UTF-8 system locale, `new FileReader(path)` and `String.getBytes()` would use the native Windows codepage (e.g., windows-1252 or a DBCS codepage like MS932/Shift-JIS depending on locale). From JDK 18 onward (so this applies when moving to JDK 21), both default to UTF-8 instead. This can silently change how non-ASCII bytes are read/written, causing mojibake or data corruption if files were written under the old default. You can restore old behavior temporarily via `-Dfile.encoding=COMPAT`, but the real fix is to specify charsets explicitly (`InputStreamReader(..., StandardCharsets.UTF_8)` or the platform charset explicitly).

rows.baseline_answer_full: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (without CONCURRENTLY) acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the materialized view. ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with every other lock mode, including the ACCESS SHARE lock that a plain SELECT needs. As a result, any SELECT issued against the view while the refresh transaction is running will be blocked and must wait in the lock queue until the REFRESH command's transaction commits (or rolls back) and releases the lock. There is no concurrent read access during this window — the view is effectively unavailable for querying for the duration of the refresh. To avoid this stall, use REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY instead, which takes a weaker EXCLUSIVE lock and allows concurrent SELECTs to proceed, at the cost of requiring a unique index on the view and generally taking longer to run than the non-concurrent refresh.

rows.governed_answer_full: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW without CONCURRENTLY acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the materialized view. This is the strictest lock mode in PostgreSQL and conflicts with every other lock mode, including ACCESS SHARE, which is what a plain SELECT takes. As a result, a SELECT issued against the materialized view while the refresh is running will block and wait until the refresh transaction commits (or rolls back). The dashboard will stall for the duration of the refresh. If concurrent read access during refresh is required, the operator should use REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY instead, which takes a less restrictive lock (roughly EXCLUSIVE, not ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) and allows concurrent SELECTs to proceed, though it requires a unique index on the materialized view and is typically slower because it computes a diff.

rows.baseline_answer_full:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the table. This mode doesn't conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE (the lock INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE take), so concurrent DML proceeds normally - only conflicts with other DDL-ish operations (another CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM FULL, ALTER TABLE, etc.). 'Non-blocking' is accurate here.

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY takes an EXCLUSIVE lock on the materialized view. EXCLUSIVE conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE, so if DML were attempted it would block. But materialized views aren't directly writable via INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE regardless of locking - they're read-only except through REFRESH. So the real effect of CONCURRENTLY here is allowing concurrent SELECT (ACCESS SHARE) reads, which a plain REFRESH (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) would block. Calling it 'non-blocking' for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE is misleading/inapplicable; it should be described as 'allows concurrent reads' instead.

rows.governed_answer_full:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY acquires a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the target table. This mode conflicts with itself and with other DDL-ish locks (VACUUM FULL, ALTER TABLE, another CONCURRENTLY build) but does not conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE, so concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (and SELECT) proceed normally — 'non-blocking' is an accurate description for DML here.

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY acquires an ExclusiveLock on the materialized view (versus AccessExclusiveLock for a plain REFRESH). However, materialized views are not directly writable — you cannot INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into one — so the 'concurrent DML' question doesn't apply. What CONCURRENTLY actually buys you is that SELECT (AccessShareLock) can still run against the matview while the refresh proceeds, since plain REFRESH's AccessExclusiveLock would block even reads. So the ticket's 'non-blocking' claim is valid for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY w.r.t. writes, but for the REFRESH statement it should instead be framed as 'non-blocking for reads' — there's no DML to block in the first place.

rows.baseline_answer_full: (a) Yes — TRUNCATE is transactional in PostgreSQL. If the transaction containing TRUNCATE (and the subsequent COPY) rolls back, the truncation is undone and the original table contents are restored, since PostgreSQL implements TRUNCATE by creating a new relfilenode and dropping the old one only at commit. So the data-reload script's reliance on rollback-to-restore is valid. (b) It is NOT MVCC-safe with respect to concurrent transactions: unlike DELETE, TRUNCATE does not produce row versions that older snapshots can still see. A concurrent transaction with an existing snapshot that tries to access the table after the TRUNCATE commits will see an empty table (or get an error depending on isolation level/lock wait), not the pre-truncate rows — this is explicitly called out in PostgreSQL docs as a concurrency hazard. (c) TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table, blocking all concurrent reads and writes until the transaction commits or rolls back.

rows.governed_answer_full:
(a) Yes. In PostgreSQL, TRUNCATE is transactional/DDL-safe: it runs inside the enclosing transaction, and if that transaction rolls back, the truncation (and any COPY after it) is undone, leaving the table exactly as it was before. This is a well-documented PostgreSQL-specific guarantee (unlike some other databases where TRUNCATE is auto-committing). So the data-reload script's reliance on rollback-to-restore is valid in PostgreSQL. (b) No. TRUNCATE is not MVCC-safe with respect to concurrent transactions that already hold a snapshot taken before the TRUNCATE commits: PostgreSQL physically truncates/removes the table's storage files rather than creating MVCC-visible delete markers, so a concurrent transaction with an older snapshot that tries to read the table after the TRUNCATE commits can get inconsistent results or errors (historically this could even surface as 'could not open file' errors for serializable/repeatable-read transactions that started before the truncate). PostgreSQL's documentation explicitly warns about this non-MVCC behavior. (c) TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table, blocking essentially all other concurrent access (reads and writes) until the transaction commits or rolls back.

deep_consensus_result_object.governed_answer:
(a) Yes. In PostgreSQL, TRUNCATE is transactional/DDL-safe: it runs inside the enclosing transaction, and if that transaction rolls back, the truncation (and any COPY after it) is undone, leaving the table exactly as it was before. This is a well-documented PostgreSQL-specific guarantee (unlike some other databases where TRUNCATE is auto-committing). So the data-reload script's reliance on rollback-to-restore is valid in PostgreSQL. (b) No. TRUNCATE is not MVCC-safe with respect to concurrent transactions that already hold a snapshot taken before the TRUNCATE commits: PostgreSQL physically truncates/removes the table's storage files rather than creating MVCC-visible delete markers, so a concurrent transaction with an older snapshot that tries to read the table after the TRUNCATE commits can get inconsistent results or errors (historically this could even surface as 'could not open file' errors for serializable/repeatable-read transactions that started before the truncate). PostgreSQL's documentation explicitly warns about this non-MVCC behavior. (c) TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table, blocking essentially all other concurrent access (reads and writes) until the transaction commits or rolls back.

rows.baseline_answer_full: No, T1 does not apply its update to that row. In READ COMMITTED, when an UPDATE blocks on a row locked by a concurrent transaction, it waits for that transaction to finish. If the blocking transaction commits, PostgreSQL does not simply proceed with the original snapshot's row version — it performs an EvalPlanQual (EPQ) check: it fetches the newest committed version of the row and re-evaluates the UPDATE's WHERE clause against that new version. Here, T2 changed status to 'closed', so the predicate status = 'open' no longer holds, and PostgreSQL silently skips updating that row (it is excluded from the result set, not an error). This means simple conditional counter updates are already safe from applying stale-predicate writes under READ COMMITTED; FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE would mainly matter for cross-row invariants or avoiding the wait/retry pattern itself, not this single-row predicate race.

rows.governed_answer_full:
No. In READ COMMITTED, when T1's UPDATE finds the target row locked by T2, it blocks on that row's lock. Once T2 commits, T1 doesn't blindly proceed with its original snapshot of the row — PostgreSQL re-fetches the latest committed version of that row and re-evaluates the UPDATE's WHERE clause against it (the EvalPlanQual mechanism). Since T2 set status='closed', the predicate status='open' now fails for that row, so T1 silently skips it — no increment is applied, no error is raised. (If T2 had instead rolled back, T1 would re-check against the original 'open' row and proceed to update it.) This recheck-on-conflict behavior means a plain UPDATE...WHERE in READ COMMITTED is already safe against this particular race for a single targeted row; FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE would mainly be needed for read-then-write logic split across separate statements, or to avoid lost updates in multi-row/aggregate scenarios.

A.verdict: No — PostgreSQL rechecks the WHERE clause against the post-commit row version, so the now-'closed' row is skipped and not updated.
A.answer: No. In READ COMMITTED, when T1's UPDATE finds the target row locked by T2, it blocks on that row's lock. Once T2 commits, T1 doesn't blindly proceed with its original snapshot of the row — PostgreSQL re-fetches the latest committed version of that row and re-evaluates the UPDATE's WHERE clause against it (the EvalPlanQual mechanism). Since T2 set status='closed', the predicate status='open' now fails for that row, so T1 silently skips it — no increment is applied, no error is raised. (If T2 had instead rolled back, T1 would re-check against the original 'open' row and proceed to update it.) This recheck-on-conflict behavior means a plain UPDATE...WHERE in READ COMMITTED is already safe against this particular race for a single targeted row; FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE would mainly be needed for read-then-write logic split across separate statements, or to avoid lost updates in multi-row/aggregate scenarios.

B.answer: No. In default READ COMMITTED, T1's UPDATE first finds rows matching WHERE as of command start, then waits on T2's lock. When T2 commits, PostgreSQL re-reads the latest committed version of that row and re-evaluates T1's WHERE clause (EvalPlanQual). Status is now 'closed', so the predicate fails and T1 skips the row; n is left unchanged. If T2 had rolled back, T1 would update the original 'open' row. If SET had still applied, expressions such as n = n + 1 would use the latest version. Skipping a no-longer-open row is the intended READ COMMITTED behavior for a conditional counter; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE is only needed if you must serialize, wait-and-apply, or abort on conflict rather than skip.

rows.baseline_answer_full: Because both methods use REQUIRED and the inner bean call goes through its own transactional proxy, the inner transaction joins the single existing physical transaction (1 physical transaction total). When the inner method throws a RuntimeException, Spring's transaction interceptor marks the transaction rollback-only via setRollbackOnly() before the exception propagates to the outer method. The outer method's catch block swallows the exception and returns normally, so no exception leaves the outer method body — but at commit time the outer transactional proxy sees the rollback-only flag and refuses to commit. Instead of committing, it rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException to the outer method's caller. Net effect: no data is committed, and the caller receives an exception they never expected given the try/catch appeared to handle the failure.

rows.governed_answer_full: Because both methods use the default propagation (REQUIRED) and are invoked via Spring proxies, the inner call joins the outer method's existing transaction — there is only ONE physical transaction. When the inner bean's @Transactional interceptor sees the RuntimeException (unchecked, matches default rollback rule), it calls setRollbackOnly() on the shared transaction before rethrowing. The outer method catches that exception, logs it, and returns normally. At method exit, the outer proxy's advice sees normal return and attempts to commit — but finds the transaction already marked rollback-only, so instead of committing it rolls back and throws org.springframework.transaction.UnexpectedRollbackException to the outer method's caller. The caller never sees the original RuntimeException, only UnexpectedRollbackException. So: no commit; caller sees UnexpectedRollbackException; 1 physical transaction.

rows.baseline_answer_full: Spring's @Configuration default is proxyBeanMethods = true. This works via CGLIB: Spring subclasses the @Configuration class and intercepts each @Bean method call. When one @Bean method calls another @Bean method directly in Java, the CGLIB proxy intercepts that call, checks the BeanFactory for an existing instance of that bean, and returns the shared singleton instead of letting the raw method body execute again — this preserves singleton semantics even for plain in-class method calls ('full' configuration mode). When proxyBeanMethods = false, no CGLIB proxy is created ('lite' mode); the class is used as-is, so a direct method call just executes the plain Java method body, constructing a brand-new object each time rather than fetching the container-managed singleton. This breaks any inter-bean reference pattern relying on singleton semantics via direct calls — such calls should instead use method parameters (Spring injects the singleton) or be restructured. The tradeoff: faster startup/less CGLIB overhead vs. losing this implicit singleton-preserving behavior.

rows.governed_answer_full:
By default, proxyBeanMethods is true. Spring CGLIB-subclasses the @Configuration class, so each @Bean method call is intercepted: the proxy checks the BeanFactory and returns the existing singleton (or correctly scoped instance) instead of running the method body again, unless it genuinely needs to create it. This makes inter-bean method calls behave like bean references, preserving singleton semantics and scoping even with plain Java calls.

When proxyBeanMethods = false, no CGLIB proxy is created (the config class is 'lite' mode). A direct method call just executes the Java method body normally, constructing a brand-new object each time, bypassing the container. So the caller gets a newly constructed instance, not the managed singleton — any @Autowired-injected dependencies on that new instance would also be missing unless manually wired. You lose this cross-bean-reference safety net in exchange for faster startup (no CGLIB subclassing) and compatibility with final classes/native-image-friendly reflection-free config.

UNRESOLVED -- the two models did not settle these:
- default_behavior_proxyBeanMethods_true: A='shared singleton returned' vs B='true'
- tradeoff_of_proxyBeanMethods_false: A='faster startup, no reflection-free native-image friendliness, but loses inter-bean-call singleton safety' vs B='newly constructed instance'

Prior to JDK 24, a virtual thread blocking (e.g., on I/O or another lock) while holding a monitor via synchronized would pin its carrier platform thread, which is why the 2023 article recommended migrating to java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock. JEP 491, delivered in JDK 24, changed the synchronized implementation so virtual threads blocking inside synchronized methods/blocks no longer pin the carrier. If the service is already on JDK 24+, this pinning cause is gone, so code already migrated to ReentrantLock does not need to be reverted (it still works correctly, just may be unnecessary for this specific reason now). However, pinning has not been eliminated entirely — other causes (e.g., blocking inside native code/JNI calls, or certain legacy VM-level operations) can still pin a carrier thread. The engineer should first confirm the JDK version in production before committing to the large migration.

rows.baseline_answer_full: Starting with JDK 18, JEP 400 ('UTF-8 by Default') made UTF-8 the default charset across all platforms, including Windows. So Charset.defaultCharset() returns UTF-8 even though the system codepage is windows-1252 (Cp1252); the OS codepage is no longer consulted for this. JEP 400 is the specification change, delivered in JDK 18. Passing -Dfile.encoding=<value> on the java command line is an officially supported way to configure file.encoding (and thus influence default-charset-derived behavior), though Charset.defaultCharset() itself is specified to be UTF-8 unless overridden via the special COMPAT token. To restore the previous locale/codepage-dependent behavior (native encoding, e.g. windows-1252 on this system), set -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT. For the FileWriter scenario, best practice is still to avoid relying on default charset and instead use explicit-charset constructors (e.g., new OutputStreamWriter(..., StandardCharsets.UTF_8) or the JDK 11+ FileWriter(file, Charset) overload) so behavior is deterministic across JDK versions and platforms.

rows.governed_answer_full:
Starting with JDK 18, Charset.defaultCharset() always returns UTF-8, independent of the OS/locale/codepage (so on this Windows box with codepage windows-1252 it still returns UTF-8, not windows-1252). This behavior was specified by JEP 400 'UTF-8 by Default' in JDK 18. Setting -Dfile.encoding on the java command line remains a supported configuration mechanism, but per JEP 400 the only supported values are 'UTF-8' (the default) and 'COMPAT'. Passing -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT restores the pre-JDK-18 locale-dependent default charset behavior (i.e., it would again resolve to windows-1252 on this system). Note sun.jnu.encoding (used for file names/args) is a separate, still locale-dependent property. For the FileWriter scenario, prefer explicit charsets (e.g., new FileWriter(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) over relying on defaults or COMPAT.

rows.baseline_answer_full: ConcurrentHashMap provides weakly consistent iterators: concurrent puts/removes during iteration never throw ConcurrentModificationException (unlike HashMap). However, an Iterator instance itself is not thread-safe to share across threads—each Iterator has internal mutable state (next node, current bucket, etc.) with no synchronization, so concurrent calls to next()/remove() on the same iterator from multiple threads can corrupt that state or throw spurious exceptions (e.g., NoSuchElementException). Each thread should obtain its own iterator via map.entrySet().iterator(). Regarding size(): it returns an approximation—CHM computes it from per-segment/counter cells that are updated without full locking, so under concurrent modification size() can be stale or inconsistent with the actual entry count at any instant. It's fine for monitoring/heuristics but should not be relied on for exact program control like triggering an exact-batch-size action; use an explicit counter (e.g., AtomicInteger/LongAdder) or a blocking/bounded structure (e.g., process-and-drain pattern) if precise batch semantics are required.

rows.governed_answer_full:
ConcurrentHashMap's iterator is weakly consistent: it never throws ConcurrentModificationException, even with concurrent puts/removes. It reflects the state of the map at iterator creation and may (but is not guaranteed to) reflect later modifications; it won't throw, won't necessarily see every update, and won't see the same element twice. Sharing a single Iterator instance across multiple threads is unsafe because Iterator implementations (including CHM's) are not thread-safe themselves — concurrent calls to hasNext()/next() on the same iterator instance can race and corrupt the iterator's internal traversal state, even though the backing map is thread-safe. Each thread should get its own iterator via map.entrySet().iterator() etc. size() on CHM is an approximation under concurrent modification — it's computed via a probabilistic/sum-of-counters algorithm and may be inaccurate at the instant of the call. Using `if (map.size() >= BATCH)` as a precise trigger is unreliable; use isEmpty()-style checks only when exactness isn't required, or use an external counter (AtomicInteger/AtomicLong) for accurate batch triggering.

NOT CROSS-CHECKED -- no second model ever examined these:
- CHM iterator CME: 'false' (unparsed)
- sharing single iterator across threads: 'false' (unparsed)
- CHM size() accuracy under concurrency: 'approximate' (unparsed)
- batch trigger using size(): 'unreliable' (unparsed)

A.verdict: No CME ever; iterator is weakly consistent and sharing it across threads is unsafe for other reasons; size() is a snapshot-ish estimate, not reliable for exact control flow.
A.answer: ConcurrentHashMap's iterator is weakly consistent: it never throws ConcurrentModificationException, even with concurrent puts/removes. It reflects the state of the map at iterator creation and may (but is not guaranteed to) reflect later modifications; it won't throw, won't necessarily see every update, and won't see the same element twice. Sharing a single Iterator instance across multiple threads is unsafe because Iterator implementations (including CHM's) are not thread-safe themselves — concurrent calls to hasNext()/next() on the same iterator instance can race and corrupt the iterator's internal traversal state, even though the backing map is thread-safe. Each thread should get its own iterator via map.entrySet().iterator() etc. size() on CHM is an approximation under concurrent modification — it's computed via a probabilistic/sum-of-counters algorithm and may be inaccurate at the instant of the call. Using `if (map.size() >= BATCH)` as a precise trigger is unreliable; use isEmpty()-style checks only when exactness isn't required, or use an external counter (AtomicInteger/AtomicLong) for accurate batch triggering.

rows.governed_answer_full: Per RFC 9111, Cache-Control: no-cache on a response does NOT forbid a cache from storing it. no-cache means the response may be stored, but MUST NOT be reused to satisfy a subsequent request without first successfully revalidating it with the origin server (i.e., a conditional request that gets a fresh validation, such as a 304 or a new 200). So caches (including shared/intermediary caches) can still retain a full copy of the personal data on disk or in memory indefinitely; they just can't serve it from cache without checking back. The directive that actually forbids storage is no-store: a response with Cache-Control: no-store MUST NOT be stored by any cache (private or shared) in any non-volatile storage, and should not be retained even in volatile memory longer than needed to transmit it. For an authenticated page with personal data that must not be retained, the reviewer should use no-store (commonly paired with private) rather than no-cache. So: no, no-cache does not forbid storage; no-store does; and no, a no-cache response may not be reused without successful revalidation against the origin.

rows.baseline_answer_full: Per RFC 9110, 401 Unauthorized applies when a request lacks valid authentication credentials (despite the 'Unauthorized' name, it really means 'Unauthenticated'). 403 Forbidden applies when the server understood the request and refuses to authorize it, regardless of credentials. So the described gateway behavior is indeed backwards: a missing bearer token (no/invalid credentials) should yield 401, and insufficient scope (authenticated but not permitted) should yield 403. On mandatory headers: RFC 9110 §15.5.2 states a 401 response MUST include a WWW-Authenticate header field containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource. 403 has no mandated response header field in RFC 9110 — a WWW-Authenticate field MAY be included but is optional (RFC 9110 §15.5.4).

rows.governed_answer_full:
Per RFC 9110 §15.5.2, status code 401 (Unauthorized) applies when the request lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. Per §15.5.4, 403 (Forbidden) applies when the server understood the request but refuses to authorize it (e.g., the credentials are valid but insufficient, such as wrong scope/permissions). A 401 response MUST include a WWW-Authenticate header field containing at least one challenge. No header field is mandated on a 403 response. Given this, the gateway's behavior described is backwards: a missing bearer token (no credentials at all) should return 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge, while insufficient scope (valid credentials, inadequate permission) should return 403.

UNRESOLVED -- the two models did not settle these:
- 401 status code meaning: A='401 Unauthorized = missing/invalid authentication credentials' vs B='lacks valid authentication credentials'
- 403 status code meaning: A='403 Forbidden = understood but refused to authorize' vs B='understood but refuses to fulfil'
- mandatory header on 401: A='WWW-Authenticate' vs B='false'

NOT ESTABLISHED (left as UNKNOWN rather than guessed):
- mandatory header on 403

rows.baseline_answer_full: RFC 9700 (BCP 240) treats the two grants differently. For the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant, the RFC uses the strongest prohibition keyword: clients 'MUST NOT' use it, reflecting that it is considered obsolete and insecure (it exposes the end-user credentials directly to the client, defeats the purpose of delegated authorization, and is incompatible with multi-factor/external authentication). For the implicit grant (response_type=token and other response types that return access tokens directly from the authorization endpoint), the RFC uses a weaker, non-absolute keyword: clients 'SHOULD NOT' use it, because of token leakage/replay risks via the URI fragment and lack of client authentication. Per RFC 2119 semantics, SHOULD NOT permits deviation if the implications are understood and justified by specific circumstances, whereas MUST NOT is an absolute prohibition. So no, the levels are not the same. Practical implication for your review: the mobile app's use of ROPC is a hard violation of the BCP and should be remediated/removed; the SPA's use of implicit flow is a strong recommendation against, but could potentially be defended on a documented, time-boxed basis with compensating controls (e.g., strict redirect URI validation, short token lifetimes, migration plan to Authorization Code + PKCE) — though RFC 9700's clear guidance is to migrate away from implicit as well, since Authorization Code with PKCE is the recommended replacement for both native/mobile and SPA use cases.

rows.governed_answer_full: RFC 9700 treats the two grants differently. For the resource owner password credentials (ROPC) grant, the RFC uses the strongest prohibition: it states the grant 'MUST NOT be used' (and should be omitted from new implementations), reflecting that no practical compensating control is accepted as sufficient given its exposure of raw credentials to the client and incompatibility with multi-factor/federated auth. For the implicit grant (and other response types that return access tokens directly from the authorization endpoint), the RFC uses a weaker recommendation: clients 'SHOULD NOT' use the implicit grant, due to token leakage/replay risks via browser history, referrer headers, and no client authentication. SHOULD NOT permits exceptions when justified and mitigated, whereas MUST NOT is an absolute prohibition. So: the mobile app's password grant has no defensible path and must be removed; the SPA's implicit flow is disfavored but RFC 9700 leaves room to argue for retention with compensating controls, though migrating to authorization code + PKCE is the clearly preferred remediation.

Context:
A security review of two legacy integrations: a mobile app using the password grant, and an SPA using the implicit flow. The question is which must be removed and which may be argued for with compensating controls.
deep_consensus_result_object.status_explanation: Every material claim is now AGREED, CORRECTED_AND_AGREED or CONFIRMED_ONE_SIDED after one review round, with nothing left uncompared.
deep_consensus_result_object.verdict: RFC 9700 bans the password grant with MUST NOT, but only discourages the implicit grant with SHOULD NOT — the two are not the same strength.
deep_consensus_result_object.governed_answer: RFC 9700 treats the two grants differently. For the resource owner password credentials (ROPC) grant, the RFC uses the strongest prohibition: it states the grant 'MUST NOT be used' (and should be omitted from new implementations), reflecting that no practical compensating control is accepted as sufficient given its exposure of raw credentials to the client and incompatibility with multi-factor/federated auth. For the implicit grant (and other response types that return access tokens directly from the authorization endpoint), the RFC uses a weaker recommendation: clients 'SHOULD NOT' use the implicit grant, due to token leakage/replay risks via browser history, referrer headers, and no client authentication. SHOULD NOT permits exceptions when justified and mitigated, whereas MUST NOT is an absolute prohibition. So: the mobile app's password grant has no defensible path and must be removed; the SPA's implicit flow is disfavored but RFC 9700 leaves room to argue for retention with compensating controls, though migrating to authorization code + PKCE is the clearly preferred remediation.

B.verdict: RFC 9700 forbids ROPC with MUST NOT and only discourages implicit with SHOULD NOT; they are not the same.
B.answer: RFC 9700 (BCP 240) says the resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used (Section 2.4). Clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type token) unless access-token injection is prevented and the listed leakage vectors are mitigated (Section 2.1.2). The keywords differ: MUST NOT vs SHOULD NOT. ROPC has no allowed exception and must be removed. Implicit is a recommendation with an explicit unless-clause, so compensating controls can be argued.
